title: Reasoning or Rationalization? Moral Robustness as a Frontier for Non-Verifiable Reasoning in LLMs
claim: A controlled multi-turn simulation framework perturbs structure, user view and context, and reveals that no model is fully robust.
layout: 2 panels: left nested framework boxes with arrows, right criteria-by-model checkmark table
description: The left panel, titled Simulation Framework, shows nested rounded boxes of simulated user and robot-model chat turns. Structural Perturbations compare Single-Turn and Multi-Turn conversations. Colored chips (gray Scenario, blue Pro, red Con) are connected by curved arrows that show order swaps. An orange box labeled User Moral View Injection feeds into the conversation through an arrow. A maroon-purple box labeled Contextual: + New Consideration holds an irrelevant turn and a relevant contrarian turn. A gray arrow leads down to a Final Question box. The right panel is a table of robustness profiles. Its rows are the manipulations (Contextual, User Moral View Injection, Order, Duration), and its columns are four LLMs. Green checks and red crosses fill the cells. Most cells are red, which shows that no model passes every criterion.
caption: We present a multi-turn, experimentally controlled framework for evaluating the robustness of moral reasoning in simulating user-model conversations (left). In our framework, a model is morally robust if its judgments remain invariant to: morally-irrelevant structural perturbations (order of considerations pro & con and duration with which these are presented - single-turn or multi-turn), a user moral view injection (for / against), and irrelevant contextual perturbations (including irrelevant new considerations). Example conversations are included in Appendix [ref]. We present profiles for each LLM tested (right), and find that none pass all the moral robustness criteria.
abstract: As LLMs increasingly serve in advisory and deliberative roles, users rely on them for non-verifiable reasoning in domains lacking objective ground truths. However, traditional evaluations of LLM reasoning focus almost exclusively on fact-based domains, such as mathematics and science, leaving uncertainty over whether and to what degree models can handle ambiguous, subjective, or value-laden problems over time. To address this concern, we examine moral reasoning as a paradigmatic subdomain of non-verifiable reasoning. We define moral robustness as a model’s capacity to exhibit sound moral reasoning across time and contexts, and we introduce a scalable, adversarial, multi-turn evaluation framework to empirically measure this capability. We simulate 128,000 user-agent moral deliberations across ten frontier LLMs, varying premise relevance, premise order, conversation duration, and the user’s stated moral view. We find that models successfully ignore morally-irrelevant distractors, but shift their verdicts by as much as 7.5%, on average, towards the user’s preferred moral view, and vary their reasoning depending on factors such as order (flipping final moral verdicts by order in 15-31% of the cases) and duration (altering moral verdicts between single-turn and multi-turn in 16-31% of the cases). Our analysis indicates that models tailor not just their final verdicts but their underlying justifications to align with a user’s moral viewpoint — a failure mode we characterize as moral deliberative sycophancy.
